data.content_ref: inline:The target claims the methodological rule 'selects the theory with the highest informational content and severest test survival' as a coherent, defensible selection criterion on Popper's terms. But these two criteria can conflict: the theory with the highest informational content (the most falsifiable, making the riskiest predictions) may have been falsified, while a theory that survived severe tests may have done so precisely because its lower content exposed it to fewer falsification risks. Popper's framework provides no total ordering or priority rule to resolve such conflicts — in his mature work he acknowledged that degrees of corroboration are not always comparable across theories. The target presents 'highest informational content and severest test survival' as a single conjunctive criterion that cleanly 'selects' a theory, but when the criteria diverge the rule is incomplete and cannot perform the selection it claims to perform. Therefore the assertion that this is 'defensible on Popper's terms' as a functioning methodological rule overstates what Popper's framework actually delivers: it describes two desirable properties that Popper never showed jointly determine a unique, comparable preference ordering.
